title: Uber India Launches In-App Video Recording and Ambulance Assistance in Industry-First Safety Push
excerpt: The 'Record My Ride' feature enables encrypted in-cab video on drivers' phones, while a Dial 4242 partnership brings one-tap ambulance access — Nitin Gadkari lauds the road safety initiative
body:
Uber India has launched two safety features that mark firsts for the ride-hailing industry in the country: an in-app video recording tool called "Record My Ride" and direct ambulance assistance through a partnership with medical logistics provider Dial 4242.

The announcements, made on Tuesday, were lauded by Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari, who praised Uber's road safety push. The features build on a suite of safety innovations the company has rolled out in India over the past year, including audio recording, women rider preference, helmet selfie verification, and seatbelt reminders.

## How 'Record My Ride' Works

The Record My Ride feature allows Uber drivers to securely record encrypted in-cab video using their own smartphones during trips. If a driver feels unsafe at any point, they can activate the recording through the Uber app's safety shield. Riders receive an in-trip notification when video recording is active, serving as both a transparency measure and a deterrent against misconduct.

The recordings are double-encrypted and stored locally on the driver's device. Neither Uber nor any third party can access the footage unless the driver chooses to share it as part of a safety report. Recordings are automatically deleted after one week if not shared, addressing privacy concerns while maintaining accountability.

The feature was first piloted in 10 Indian cities — Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Pune, Hyderabad, Chandigarh, Kolkata, Jaipur, and Lucknow — beginning in May 2026, according to TechCrunch. It has now been rolled out nationally.


![Union Minister — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2f/Modi_3.0_Ministry.jpg)



> **""Even female passengers traveling late at night insist that we follow the route they want instead of what's shown on the map."**



The tool addresses a persistent pain point for drivers in the Indian market. Half a dozen Uber drivers in the Delhi-NCR region told TechCrunch that they sometimes face misconduct from riders and, in some cases, are threatened with false complaints — allegations that can lead to penalties or account suspensions. "Even female passengers traveling late at night insist that we follow the route they want instead of what's shown on the map. If we refuse, they threaten to file false complaints," one driver said.

## Ambulance Integration: A First for Ride-Hailing

The ambulance assistance feature, developed in partnership with Dial 4242, allows both riders and drivers to quickly request medical support following an accident directly through the Uber app. Rather than scrambling to find emergency contacts or navigate multiple apps in a crisis, users can summon an ambulance with a few taps within the same interface they used to book their ride.

Dial 4242 is one of India's largest medical logistics providers, operating a network of ambulances across major metropolitan areas. The integration brings professional emergency medical services within the ride-hailing ecosystem for the first time in India — a country where road accidents claim approximately 170,000 lives annually, according to government data.

## The Broader Safety Push

Uber's latest features are part of a deliberate strategy to differentiate on safety in India's fiercely competitive ride-hailing market, where it competes with homegrown rival Ola and a growing roster of regional players. The company has positioned safety as a baseline expectation rather than a premium add-on.


![Road Transport — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Nissan_Tsuru_taxi_Mexico_Ciudad.jpg/3840px-Nissan_Tsuru_taxi_Mexico_Ciudad.jpg)


"As expectations evolve, we hope the industry will rise up to meet them," an Uber executive said, signalling that the company views its safety innovations as a competitive moat that it wants rivals to match — a rising-tide approach that also deflects regulatory pressure.

Other safety features already live on the platform include RideCheck (which uses sensors to detect unusual trip activity like unexpected stops or route deviations), customisable trip-verification PINs, a "Don't Type & Drive" feature for drivers, and a 24/7 Safety Line. The women rider preference feature, which allows female riders to request female drivers, has been particularly popular in Indian cities where safety concerns disproportionately affect women commuters.

## What It Means for Riders in India

For the millions of Indians — and visitors — who rely on Uber daily, the new features address two of the most visceral concerns about ride-hailing: personal safety during the ride, and what happens if something goes seriously wrong. The video recording creates a mutual accountability framework where both drivers and riders know their behaviour is documented, while the ambulance integration provides a critical safety net for the worst-case scenario.

The features are also relevant for the millions of NRIs who use Uber when visiting India. Ride-hailing safety standards in India have historically lagged behind those in the US, UK, and other markets where Uber operates. Features like Record My Ride bring the Indian experience closer to parity with global standards — a comfort factor for diaspora travellers navigating the often chaotic traffic conditions of Indian cities.

Privacy advocates will want to monitor how the encrypted video data is handled at scale, particularly in a market without a comprehensive data protection law in force. Uber says recordings can only be accessed by the driver and only shared voluntarily — but the company has also acknowledged that recordings may be provided to law enforcement with appropriate legal process or in emergency situations.

For now, however, the consensus among drivers and safety advocates appears to be that the benefits of documentation outweigh the privacy trade-offs — particularly in a market where "he said, she said" disputes between drivers and riders have historically been resolved in favour of the paying customer.
